subsection: 6. Increasing international involvement: the UN and the EEC

notes.h: Background: neutrality, the Cold War and the road to the UN
notes.b: To see why Ireland's entry to international bodies was slow and then fast, you need three pieces of background: its record in the League of Nations, its neutrality, and the Cold War split of the world into two camps.
points: Ireland was a member of the League of Nations (the interwar association of states) from 1923 to 1946, and was neutral in the Second World War (1939-45), which Irish people called 'the Emergency'. This is why it was not a stranger to international bodies in 1946.
That wartime neutrality shaped how other states saw Ireland in 1946, which is why it became an obstacle when Ireland first asked to join the United Nations.

The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States-led West and the Soviet bloc. NATO, the Western military alliance, was founded in April 1949. This is why the Soviet Union and the West treated each new UN member as a point scored.

The UN Security Council has five permanent members (the United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France and China), and each holds a veto, meaning one of them can block a decision on its own. This power decided Ireland's first application.
Ireland declined to join NATO in 1949, giving partition (the division of the island) as its reason, and kept to a policy of military neutrality: belonging to no military bloc.
In the 1950s Britain was Ireland's main market for exports, so any British decision about Europe would force an Irish one. This mattered once the EEC appeared.
notes.tip: For a 'isolation to international involvement' essay, learn the sequence as a spine: 1946 veto, 1955 entry, 1960 Congo, 1961 EEC application, 1973 entry. Link neutrality to peacekeeping.

notes.b: Ireland wanted to join the UN as soon as it was founded, but the Cold War kept it out for nearly a decade. It was outside the UN until 1955, even though it had been in the League of Nations and other European bodies.
points: Ireland applied for UN membership in 1946, but the Soviet Union used its veto in the Security Council, citing Ireland's neutrality in the Second World War and the lack of diplomatic relations between the two states.

The deadlock over new members lasted until 1955, when a package deal in the General Assembly (the UN's body of all member states) allowed sixteen states to be admitted together, so neither side had to approve a state it disliked on its own.

Ireland was admitted on 14 December 1955, alongside states as varied as Italy, Spain, Austria, Hungary and Jordan. It was a package, so Ireland came in with states from both sides of the Cold War, such as Italy and Hungary.
Ireland was neutral in the Cold War sense of belonging to no military bloc, but it was a Western, Christian democracy and generally sympathetic to the West on issues of communism.
Membership gave a small state a voice on world affairs, recognition, and a means of showing independence of Britain.
Do not confuse the vetoes: the Soviet Union vetoed Ireland in 1946 in the Security Council, whereas de Gaulle later vetoed Britain's EEC entry, a different veto in a different body.
notes.tip: Keep 1946 (application and Soviet veto) separate from 14 December 1955 (admission). Examiners credit each correct, dated statement, so give four or five short ones rather than one long story.

notes.h: Frank Aiken and an independent Irish line at the UN
notes.b: Frank Aiken, Minister for External Affairs from 1951 to 1954 and from 1957 to 1969, used the UN to pursue a policy not tied to the Western powers. His line was independent, but it was not pro-Soviet.
points: Aiken was a veteran of the War of Independence and Civil War who had been in de Valera's governments since 1932, and he led the Irish delegation to the General Assembly nearly every year. This is why he had the standing to set policy independently of the Western powers.

From 1957 Ireland would not support the American-led move to block debate on the seat of the People's Republic of China, a position that irritated Washington because it broke with the usual Western line.
In 1959 Ireland and Malaya sponsored a resolution at the UN criticising the suppression of human rights in Tibet, which shows the independent line was not simply pro-communist.
Aiken took an anti-colonial line on some issues, reflecting a small, formerly colonised state's sympathy with peoples seeking independence.
His main contribution was the effort to stop the spread of nuclear weapons (non-proliferation): Irish resolutions were introduced from 1958.
Resolution 1665 of 4 December 1961 called on all states to agree not to transfer or acquire nuclear weapons. It led to negotiations on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
The treaty opened for signature on 1 July 1968, and Ireland was the first state to sign it.
Critics said the Irish line was naive or inconsistent with Ireland's position in the West; supporters said it showed that a small state could influence world opinion.
notes.tip: Give one or two named examples of Aiken's line (China debate, the Tibet resolution of 1959, Resolution 1665 of 4 December 1961) and note the treaty came in 1968. Frank Aiken, Patrick Hillery and Frederick Boland are different people, so keep their roles straight.

notes.h: Peacekeeping: the Congo, Cyprus and Lebanon
notes.b: Peacekeeping means soldiers sent by the UN to separate fighting sides and hold a peace, rather than to fight a war. Irish soldiers served in it from 1958, and the Congo was the first major test.
points: Irish officers served as UN observers in Lebanon from 1958. This was a different, earlier mission from the later force of 1978. It was a small observer mission, so it is not the same as the larger force that came later.

The Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 and descended into disorder, with Katanga province declaring secession in July 1960. The UN sent a force, ONUC, and Irish troops joined it in July 1960.
On 8 November 1960 an Irish patrol was ambushed at Niemba in Katanga and nine soldiers were killed, the first big loss of Irish life in UN service.

In September 1961, 155 men of A Company, 35th Battalion, under Commandant Pat Quinlan, were besieged at Jadotville by Katangese forces and foreign mercenaries. After about five days, with ammunition and water short, they surrendered, and were released after some weeks.

About 6,000 Irish soldiers served in the Congo until 1964, and twenty-six lost their lives. The loss of twenty-six lives was heavy for a small army, which is why it counts in judgements on the cost of peacekeeping.

Irish troops joined the UN force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) from 1964, to keep apart the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities. The two communities were in conflict, so a neutral force was needed between them.

From 1978 an Irish battalion served with the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), set up after Israel's invasion of southern Lebanon. The force was needed because fighting in southern Lebanon had left the area unstable.
Peacekeeping linked Ireland's identity as a neutral state to practical service, and it gave the Defence Forces an important role and good reputation abroad.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Niemba (November 1960, nine killed) with Jadotville (September 1961, a siege and surrender with no Irish deaths). Name each mission with its date: ONUC, UNFICYP, UNIFIL. For judgement questions, weigh pride and reputation against the cost in lives.

notes.h: Neutrality, defence and the Irish role abroad
notes.b: Peacekeeping needed a legal basis at home, and it fitted Ireland's neutrality: a neutral state could serve the UN without joining a military alliance.
points: Ireland refused to join NATO in 1949, with partition as the stated reason, and kept to a policy of military neutrality in the Cold War. Joining would have meant allying with Britain while the island stayed divided, so partition was the reason given.
The Defence (Amendment) Act 1960 allowed the government to send Irish contingents abroad on service under the United Nations, which provided the legal basis for the Congo mission.

Peacekeeping allowed a neutral state to take part in world affairs without joining an alliance, and it became a source of national pride. For example, Irish soldiers could serve in the Congo without any alliance commitment.
Opponents of EEC entry raised in 1972 the question of whether membership would affect neutrality, and the government replied that membership did not require Ireland to join a military alliance.
notes.tip: Link neutrality to peacekeeping when asked about Irish involvement abroad: neutral status is why Irish soldiers could serve under the UN banner but not in NATO.

notes.h: Frederick Boland and the General Assembly, 1960
notes.b: Frederick Boland was a diplomat rather than a minister, and in 1960 his career brought a small, new member state a high honour at the UN.
points: Frederick Boland, formerly Secretary of the Department of External Affairs (the senior civil servant) and ambassador in London, was Ireland's permanent representative at the UN from 1956.

He was elected President of the fifteenth session of the General Assembly, which began in September 1960, an honour for a state that had joined only five years earlier. This is why the election is read as a sign of the respect Ireland had won.

The session was dominated by the crisis in the Congo and by Cold War tension, and in October 1960 Boland broke his gavel while trying to restore order during a heated exchange involving the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.

Boland's election showed the respect Ireland had gained, and the session brought more African states into the UN as colonies became independent. Many colonies were becoming independent, so the Assembly was changing in make-up.
Ireland also served on the Security Council in 1962.
notes.tip: Say only that Boland broke his gavel in a heated exchange involving Khrushchev in October 1960. Give the year 1960 and the five years since 1955 to show why the honour mattered.

notes.h: The EEC and the first application, 1961-1963
notes.b: The European Economic Community (EEC) was a common market, and Irish policy-makers soon saw that staying outside it carried risks. A common market is a group of states that trade freely without tariffs among themselves, apply a common tariff to outsiders, and allow free movement of goods, workers and capital.
points: The Treaty of Rome in 1957 created the EEC. Its six founding states were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, with a customs union and a common external tariff (one set of import taxes on goods from outside).

Britain was Ireland's main market, so when it considered joining, Irish ministers feared that British entry would leave Ireland outside a market where its farm exports would face barriers. After 1958 Ireland had also turned from protection to freer trade.

Ireland formally applied on 31 July 1961 under Taoiseach Seán Lemass, and the Dáil, the main parties and farmers' groups supported the application. The support of the Dáil, parties and farmers' groups meant the application had wide backing at home.

Supporters hoped to gain access to a large market for beef and dairy goods and to attract investment, and Lemass argued that membership would help to modernise Irish industry. Farming was a major export earner, so access to a large market mattered.

French president Charles de Gaulle vetoed British entry on 14 January 1963, which stopped negotiations, although the Irish application remained on the table. A veto by one member was enough, which means one man could halt Britain's entry and Ireland's with it.

To prepare, the government set up bodies to improve industrial competitiveness and signed the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement with Britain in 1965. This was to make Irish firms competitive, because they would face open competition inside the EEC.
notes.tip: Cause questions ask why Ireland applied in 1961: British entry, markets for farm goods, and modernisation. Do not mix the 1957 Treaty of Rome with the 1972 Treaty of Accession.

notes.h: The second application, negotiations and accession, 1967-1973
notes.b: After the first veto, Ireland tried again, and only a change of French leadership opened the way to entry. The steps run from veto to summit to treaty to referendum to membership, and they are easy to muddle.
points: Ireland, Britain, Denmark and Norway applied again in 1967, but de Gaulle vetoed British entry a second time in November 1967. Ireland was again tied to Britain's fate, which is why de Gaulle's veto stopped all of them.

After de Gaulle resigned in 1969, the Hague summit of December 1969 agreed to enlarge the community, and negotiations opened in Luxembourg in 1970. His resignation removed the main obstacle, so enlargement could go ahead.

Patrick Hillery, Minister for External Affairs from 1969 to 1973, led the Irish negotiating team; Ireland won a five-year transitional period for industry (time to adjust before facing full competition) and agreed terms on farm prices.
The transition was so that Irish industry could adjust gradually rather than face full competition at once.
The Treaty of Accession was signed in Brussels on 22 January 1972.

The government held a referendum on 10 May 1972 (the Third Amendment) to amend the Constitution to allow membership; about 83 per cent of those who voted were in favour, on a turnout of about 71 per cent.
A referendum was needed because the Constitution had to be changed before Ireland could join.
Ireland, Britain and Denmark became members on 1 January 1973, with Jack Lynch as Taoiseach; Norway's voters had rejected membership in September 1972.
Hillery became Ireland's first member of the European Commission in 1973.
notes.tip: Keep three dates apart: treaty signed January 1972, referendum May 1972, entry January 1973. Examiners credit precise figures such as about 83 per cent yes, and they penalise confusing the 1972 and 1987 referendums. Short answers on a document ask the year Ireland joined and with whom.

notes.h: Why Ireland sought EEC membership, and the opposition
notes.b: Ireland's bid to join the EEC rested on economic and political hopes, and it met organised opposition. The size of the final yes vote shows which side persuaded the public.
points: Economic motives: the failure of protection (shielding home industry with tariffs), the need for markets for beef and dairy goods beyond Britain, and the hope of attracting industry looking for access to a large market. This is why joining looked like the answer to the problems of a protected economy.

Political motives: membership would end the dependence on the British market and give a small state a seat among the major European powers. Relying on one customer left Ireland exposed, so a wider market meant more independence.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), which would pay guaranteed prices to farmers, was the strongest attraction for farmers and the Irish Farmers' Association, which supported entry. Guaranteed prices meant farmers could plan with confidence.
Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and farmers' and employers' organisations supported entry and campaigned for a yes vote.

Opponents, grouped in the Common Market Defence Campaign, argued that entry would cost sovereignty (the state's freedom to make its own laws) and neutrality, force small firms and farms out of business, and give control of the economy to foreign companies.
For example, they feared small firms could not compete with larger European companies.
Labour opposed entry in 1972, as did Sinn Féin and some trade unionists.
Raymond Crotty, an economist, was a prominent critic of the EEC.
The size of the yes vote in 1972 showed how strongly the public linked membership to economic hopes.
notes.tip: For 1972 comparison questions, give both sides with reasons: supporters (markets, CAP prices, investment) and opponents (sovereignty, neutrality, small firms and farms, foreign ownership). 'Why was the vote so large' wants the economic hopes.

notes.h: The Single European Act and the Crotty case
notes.b: In the 1980s a new European treaty raised the question of how far Ireland could hand over power without asking the people. A court case then forced a second EEC referendum, in 1987.
points: The Single European Act, signed in February 1986, aimed to complete the single market (free movement of goods, services, people and capital) by the end of 1992 and extended qualified majority voting, where a decision passes without every state agreeing, to more decisions.
This is why it was seen as a step beyond a simple trading arrangement.
It also gave a legal basis to European political cooperation, the effort of member states to coordinate foreign policy. Ireland ratified it in 1987, after the Crotty case.

Raymond Crotty, an economist and critic of the EEC, challenged the government's plan to ratify the Act. He lost in the High Court but won in the Supreme Court. He argued that ratifying would give away Irish freedom of action, so the courts were asked to decide.

On 9 April 1987 the Supreme Court ruled that the provisions on political cooperation limited the state's freedom to conduct its foreign policy, so ratification required an amendment to the Constitution.

The Tenth Amendment, approved by referendum on 26 May 1987 by about 70 per cent to 30 per cent, on a low turnout of about 44 per cent, allowed ratification. The amendment was needed because the Supreme Court had ruled the Constitution blocked ratification.
The Crotty judgment established that major transfers of power to the EEC and the EU would require a referendum in Ireland.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the referendums: 1972 (Third Amendment, to join) and 1987 (Tenth Amendment, for the Single European Act). 'Why did the Act need a referendum' needs the Supreme Court's point about foreign policy. Do not mix the Act (1986) with the Treaty of Rome (1957).

notes.h: Assessment: which mattered more, the UN or the EEC?
notes.b: Both organisations ended Ireland's isolation, but they did so in different ways. A strong answer sets them side by side and reaches a clear judgement.
points: The UN gave Ireland international recognition, a platform for independent policies on China, Tibet and nuclear weapons, and a respected peacekeeping role. It also shaped Irish identity and foreign policy.

The EEC had greater practical effect: it gave farmers guaranteed prices and access to a large market, brought regional and social funds, attracted foreign investment and reduced Ireland's dependence on Britain.
Contemporary view: supporters of the UN saw it as the best guarantee of Irish independence and neutrality, because it let a small state act without joining a bloc.
Contemporary view: supporters of the EEC saw it as the only way to modernise the economy and end dependence on Britain, since the home market and protection had failed.
Later view: historians generally judge that EEC membership had the deeper impact on Irish society and economy.
Later view: the UN involvement shaped Ireland's self-image and foreign policy and has remained an important part of its identity.
notes.tip: A narrative of one organisation with a sentence on the other scores poorly, so give balanced, dated points on each and state a judgement. Most strong answers judge that the EEC had the deeper effect, with a reason such as farm incomes, funds, investment or less dependence on Britain, while crediting the UN.

keyTerms.definition: A group of countries that trade without tariffs among themselves, apply a common tariff to outsiders and allow free movement of goods, workers and capital.
The community of six states founded by the Treaty of Rome in 1957, which Ireland, Britain and Denmark joined on 1 January 1973.
The use of lightly armed, UN-authorised troops and observers to monitor ceasefires and keep apart parties in a conflict.
The effort to stop nuclear weapons spreading to more states, to which Ireland contributed through Resolution 1665 of 1961 and the 1968 treaty.
Ireland's policy of not joining military alliances, which allowed it to take an independent line at the UN.
The power of a state to block a decision: used by the Soviet Union against Irish UN entry in 1946 and by de Gaulle against British EEC entry in 1963 and 1967.
The 1986 treaty that set out to complete the single market by 1992 and gave a legal basis to political cooperation.
The 1987 Supreme Court ruling that ratifying the Single European Act needed a constitutional amendment, because of its provisions on foreign policy cooperation.
The UN Operation in the Congo, in which Irish troops served from 1960 to 1964.
